title: 256 US Lawmakers Back July as Indian American Heritage Month
excerpt: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi's bipartisan resolution has the support of more than half the House. July marks the 1946 Luce-Celler Act, which first made people of Indian descent eligible for US citizenship.
body:
• A bipartisan House resolution to designate July as Indian American Heritage Month has 256 cosponsors — more than half of the 435-member House of Representatives.
  • Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, the lead sponsor, introduced the resolution on October 26; it has been referred to a House committee.
  • July was chosen because President Harry S. Truman signed the Luce-Celler Act on July 2, 1946, making persons of Indian descent eligible for naturalisation as US citizens.
  • As a simple House resolution, the measure would express the House's support; it would not create a federal holiday or carry the force of law.

More than half of the US House of Representatives has lined up behind a bipartisan resolution to designate July as Indian American Heritage Month. The measure, introduced by Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, honours the contributions of Indian Americans and ties the recognition to the 1946 law that first opened the door to American citizenship for people of Indian descent.

According to Krishnamoorthi's office, the resolution recognises more than 5.2 million Indian Americans and their contributions across science and medicine, technology and business, public service and the military, education, philanthropy, arts and culture, and athletics. The figure comes from US Census Bureau estimates published in 2023.

"Indian Americans have helped shape this country for generations, from breakthroughs that have saved lives and businesses that have created jobs to lifetimes of service in our military and public office."

— Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi

Why July

The choice of month is historical. On July 2, 1946, President Harry S. Truman signed the Luce-Celler Act, which made persons of Indian descent eligible for naturalisation as United States citizens, ending decades in which Indian immigrants were barred from becoming Americans. The resolution also notes that the community traces its roots to a civilisation more than 5,000 years old and describes Indian Americans as one of the most religiously diverse communities in the United States.

The context around the vote

The proposal arrives in a charged pre-midterm climate. The American Bazaar reported debate around the resolution and cited a September report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate that found anti-South Asian hate across several online platforms had risen 240% between January 2024 and June 2026. Supporters frame the measure as a statement of belonging backed by a majority of the House; the resolution number and its committee path were still being finalised in the first reports, as wire coverage noted.

What happens next

The resolution has been referred to a House committee for consideration. A simple House resolution expresses the chamber's position and does not go to the president's desk — but with 256 cosponsors from both parties, the count itself is the headline: a majority of the House is on record supporting a dedicated month recognising Indian Americans.

What the resolution credits

The text goes beyond a ceremonial nod. It credits Indian Americans with pioneering contributions to science, medicine, biomedical research, space exploration, artificial intelligence, computing and telecommunications, and notes a community that traces its roots to a civilisation more than 5,000 years old. It also describes Indian Americans as one of the most religiously diverse communities in the United States — a detail supporters say matters, because a heritage month framed around a single faith would misdescribe the community it claims to honour. Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat and one of the Indian American members of the House, built the cosponsor list across party lines, which is why the count reached a majority of the chamber rather than stopping at a symbolic bloc.
